name: Tingui-Boto

earlier_scan.source_named: Glottolog refs are ethnographic/overview only (Dantas et al. 1998, CEDI 1983); no grammar or phonology of Tingui-Boto exists

new_statements.quote: Verificou-se, na língua, que o acento lexical recai em três posições atestadas nos dados: inicial, medial e final. Constata-se também a presença de monossílabos tônicos que se soma ao quadro geral do comportamento acentual da língua em estudo. O acento inicial recai na primeira sílaba de palavras paroxítonas e proparoxítonas encontradas em Dzubukuá. [...] O acento medial, tal como o anterior, pode ser proparoxítono ou paroxítono, podendo aparecer tanto na antepenúltima sílaba de algumas palavras e na penúltima sílaba de outras. [...] O acento final ou oxítono aparece em sílabas abertas e fechadas de palavras de duas a quatro sílabas
new_statements.translation: It was found that in this language lexical stress falls in three positions attested in the data: initial, medial and final. Stressed monosyllables are also present, adding to the overall picture of the accentual behaviour of the language under study. Initial stress falls on the first syllable of paroxytone and proparoxytone words found in Dzubukuá. [...] Medial stress, like the preceding one, can be proparoxytone or paroxytone, appearing on the antepenultimate syllable of some words and on the penultimate of others. [...] Final or oxytone stress appears on open and closed syllables of words of two to four syllables.
new_statements.citation: Queiroz, José Márcio Correia de. 2012. Um estudo gramatical da língua Dzubukuá, família Karirí. Tese (Doutorado em Linguística), Universidade Federal da Paraíba, João Pessoa. 427 f. (open access: https://repositorio.ufpb.br/jspui/handle/tede/6358). NOTE: describes Dzubukuá (dzub1241 / kari1254), the language the Tingui-Botó CLAIM to use in ritual; no Tingui-Botó speech has ever been recorded.

Constata-se também a presença de monossílabos tônicos.. O acento inicial recai na primeira sílaba de palavras paroxítonas e proparoxítonas encontradas em Dzubukuá.' is on printed p. 96 = PDF p. 97 (not p. 97/PDF 98); 'O acento medial, tal como o anterior, pode ser proparoxítono ou paroxítono, podendo aparecer tanto na antepenúltima sílaba de algumas palavras e na penúltima sílaba de outras' is on printed p. 97 = PDF 98; 'O acento final ou oxítono aparece em sílabas abertas e fechadas d…
new_statements.rule_in_words: In Dzubukuá (as reconstructed from the acute/grave diacritics in Bernardo de Nantes' 1709 catechism) word stress is lexically fixed per word but not predictable: it may be final, penultimate or antepenultimate, within a three-syllable window at the right edge; open and closed syllables carry stress alike, so no weight condition is stated; paroxytones are the largest class, proparoxytones the rarest; general template (S)(S)(S)S(S)(S). Queiroz 2008 (p. 90) adds that where the catechism is inconclusive, Kipeá cognates, which are 'predominantly oxytone', decide. The description is explicitly preliminary and philological (an extinct language with no oral data).
new_statements.secondary_stress: No secondary stress described. Queiroz 2012 p. 101: in compounds, prefixed and reduplicated forms each member tends to keep its own stress ('o acento tônico tende a permanecer em cada um das formas quando elas se unem gramaticalmente'), marked by double diacritics in Nantes' text; Queiroz 2008 sec. 11.3 reads double accents as demarcating morphological boundaries.
new_statements.exceptions: Stress 'oscillations' between positions of the same word are frequent in the source text, mostly attracting stress to the penult (Queiroz 2008 sec. 11.2, pp. 93-94); one apparent pre-antepenultimate double accent 'útsótsoho' treated as a typographical lapse (Queiroz 2012 fn. 24, p. 98; Queiroz 2008 fn. 20). Only words bearing a diacritic were counted (Queiroz 2008 p. 95).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level only ('acento lexical', 'tonicidade em nível do vocábulo'); the author states that rhythm, tone, pitch and intonation cannot be recovered from the written source (Queiroz 2012 p. 96). Not citation forms of any living speaker: data are 18th-century missionary orthography.
new_statements.identity_note: ting1238 / ISO tgv is a RETIRED Glottolog bookkeeping entry ('Bookkeeping' family). The Tingui-Botó of Olho d'Água do Meio, Feira Grande (Alagoas) speak Portuguese (Glottolog comment; ISA page by V. L. Calheiros Mata). They claim to use their ancestral language, which they call 'Dzbokuá', in the secret Ouricuri ritual; Glottolog and ISA identify this as Dzubukuá = dzub1241, a dialect-level node under Kariri kari1254 (Kariri family), whose only documentation is Nantes' 1709 catechism. No linguist has recorded Tingui-Botó ritual speech; Hohenthal (1960, p. 59), who saw the group as Xokó 'Karirí', wrote that no lower-São-Francisco group kept more than a few words of doubtful linguistic value. The quoted stress statement therefore describes Dzubukuá (Queiroz 2012/2008), which the catalog ALREADY holds under kari1254 (classification lexical, same source and quote; that check recommends re-keying it to dzub1241). Ethnologue's alternate names 'Carapató/Karapató' appear to conflate the group with the separate Karapotó people of São Sebastião, AL.

readall_conflicts: The only listed work (Mamiani 1699/1877) gives fixed: final syllable stress with a few lexical exceptions, but for Kipeá Kiriri (kipe1235), not for Tingui-Boto and not for Dzubukuá (dzub1241), the variety behind the existing statement (Queiroz 2012: lexical stress, initial/medial/final). The apparent disagreement (fixed: final syllable vs lexical) is a dialect difference plus a difference in evidence: Mamiani was an ear-witness of Kipeá, whereas Queiroz reconstructs Dzubukuá stress from the accent marks in Nantes' 1709 catechism and notes that Kipeá is 'predominantemente oxítono'. Neither work describes Tingui-Boto itself, for which no linguistic data exist.

sources.note: For Dzubukuá (not Tingui-Botó; the thesis never mentions Tingui-Botó or Feira Grande): lexical stress, inferred from Nantes' 1709 acute/grave diacritics, attested in three positions - initial, medial, final - i.e. antepenult, penult or final within a right-edge three-syllable window, on open and closed syllables alike; paroxytones predominate, proparoxytones are rare; general template (S)(S)(S)S(S)(S); Quadro 8 p. 100; compounds/prefixed forms keep each member's stress (p. 101). Author calls the description preliminary and philological.

sources.note: Nothing on stress. States the entry 'has been retired and is featured here only for bookkeeping purposes'; 'There is certainly a corresponding ethnic group, but this group speaks Portuguese. They retain some of their ancestral language for ritual purposes, but this language is Dzubukuá'; Dzubukuá 'is subsumed under the (otherwise highly problematic) Kariri-Xoco [kzw] entry'.

sources.citation: Queiroz, José Márcio Correia de. 2008. Aspectos da fonologia Dzubukuá. Dissertação (Mestrado em Linguística), Universidade Federal de Pernambuco, Recife. 122 f. Ch. 11 'O acento lexical no Dzubukuá', pp. 90-95 (PDF pp. 92-97); conclusion p. 104
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: For Dzubukuá: 'Foi observada, no Dz, a ocorrência de palavras oxítonas, paroxítonas e proparoxítonas; sendo que as paroxítonas correspondem ao grupo de maior representatividade' (p. 91); up to three pretonic and two post-tonic syllables, template (S)(S)(S)S(S)(S) (p. 93); stress oscillations tend toward the penult (p. 93); where the catechism is inconclusive, Kipeá cognates ('predominantemente oxítono') decide (p. 90). Conclusion p. 104: oxytone, paroxytone and proparoxytone words occur, paroxytones predominating. No mention of Tingui-Botó.

sources.citation: Hohenthal, W. D. Jr. 1960. As tribos indígenas do médio e baixo São Francisco. Revista do Museu Paulista, n.s., 12 (57-page scan, Biblioteca Digital Curt Nimuendajú)
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Nothing on stress; no wordlist. Treats the Olho d'Água do Meio group (today's Tingui-Botó) as 'Karirí' (Xokó) and describes their February Ouricuri (pp. 63-64). On language, p. 59 (PDF 24): 'Nenhum grupo conservou mais que umas poucas palavras de sua língua aborígene, sendo essas de valor lingüístico muito duvidoso.' Also reports that Max Boudin's 1947 vocabulary from the Xokó 'Karirí' showed no resemblance to classical Kariri.
